title: Midweek Musings - September 2, 2026
author: Matthew Justin Hall
summary: In this weekly digest, Matthew Justin Hall processes Wendell Berry's death by distilling four themes from Berry's work, that place matters (citing Berry's boomer/sticker distinction), that people are not things reducible to economic production, that home and family bear more weight than modernity credits, and that real education, formation of a whole person rather than career training, has become an endangered species. From there the issue functions as a genuine curated digest rather than a bare link list: Hall summarizes and reacts to Mark Bauerlein's essay on the collapse of the literary canon in English departments (English degrees fell from one in thirteen graduates in 1970 to one in sixty today), the newly published five philosophical presuppositions of the American Enterprise Institute's AI Ethics Council, including its explicit opposition to Silicon Valley transhumanist ideology, Bonnie Kristian's pushback against what Hall calls "evangelical self-loathing," and Jonathan Imber's reflection on fifty years teaching at one institution. Each item receives Hall's own framing and reaction rather than a bare link, making the newsletter itself, as a curated weekly digest with sustained editorial commentary, independently archivable alongside any of its linked pieces.
points: Hall's four Berry themes are each backed by a specific textual anchor rather than vague tribute: the boomer/sticker distinction from the 2012 Jefferson Lecture, the title question of What Are People For?, the 69-year Berry marriage, and Berry's Trinity Forum writing on the commodification of universities.

The Bauerlein citation supplies a precise, falsifiable data point for the canon's institutional collapse: English took 'one in thirteen of all four-year degrees' in 1970 versus 'one in sixty' today, grounding the cultural argument in enrollment statistics rather than impressionistic decline-narrative.

The AI Ethics Council's five presuppositions are reproduced with enough specificity to function as a philosophical position statement in miniature, including its explicit, named opposition to Sam Altman's 'merge' project at Merge Labs as representative of transhumanist Silicon Valley ideology.

Hall closes the AI Ethics Council item on the humanities-specific warning that 'over-reliance on AI may over time hollow out both individual scholars and the practice of the scholarly vocation,' tying the digest's opening Berry tribute (formation over production) directly to its AI-ethics discussion.
quotes: Stickers on the contrary, he continued, are motivated by affection, by such love for a place and its life that they want to preserve it and remain in it. Berry's localism was increasingly out of tune with the consumerist mass culture of the digital age.

Berry was an early voice crying in the wilderness, cautioning against the commodification of education and its devolution into mere career training, with no thought to the formation of human beings as people.
In 1970, English took one in thirteen of all four-year degrees in the United States. Now, it stands at one in sixty.

We stand in opposition to the expressly transhuman or posthuman ideologies of Silicon Valley. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, has written enthusiastically about the merge between man and machine, and has co-founded a company, Merge Labs, to bring it about.

Over-reliance on AI may over time hollow out both individual scholars and the practice of the scholarly vocation, as apprenticeships that aim to attune leaders' minds to truth give way to efficient content distribution.
As a senior colleague remarked to me when I left my first full-time job for another school: You will be missed, but the institution will survive.
